subject: physics
topicDisplay: Unit 14: Waves, Sound, and Physical Optics (part 1)
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: 14.1 Properties of Wave Pulses and Waves
14.3 Boundary Behavior of Waves and Polarization

questions.q: A loudspeaker plays a steady note to a listener 5 m away in a room with still air. Which of the following travels from the loudspeaker to the listener?
options: Energy, passed along by air molecules that vibrate about fixed positions
Air molecules, pushed across the room from the loudspeaker to the ear
Sound particles, which the loudspeaker gives off and the air carries
An electromagnetic signal, which needs no air to carry it across
optionWhy: A sound wave transfers energy from the loudspeaker to the listener without transferring matter. Each air molecule vibrates back and forth about its own position and passes the disturbance on to its neighbors; the molecules near the loudspeaker never reach the listener.

A student who thinks a wave carries the material of the medium with it picks this. The loudspeaker cone pushes the nearby air back and forth, but those molecules only vibrate about their positions. The air in a room with still air does not flow to the listener; only the disturbance and its energy travel.

A student who pictures sound as a substance of its own picks this. There are no sound particles: sound is the disturbance of the air molecules themselves, a pattern of pressure changes passed from molecule to molecule.
A student who groups sound with light and radio waves picks this. Sound is a mechanical wave: it is carried by the air (or another medium) and would not reach the listener through a vacuum.
questions.explain: A sound wave transfers energy from the loudspeaker to the listener without transferring matter. Each air molecule vibrates back and forth about its own position and passes the disturbance on to its neighbors; the molecules near the loudspeaker never reach the listener.

questions.q: A long slinky is stretched along a table. A student repeatedly pushes one end forward along the slinky's length and pulls it back, sending a wave along the slinky. How does one coil in the middle of the slinky move as the wave passes?
options: Side to side across the table, perpendicular to the slinky's length
Along the slinky to the far end, carried there by the passing wave
Back and forth along the slinky's length, about a fixed position
Along a wavy path, following the shape of the wave as it passes
optionWhy: A student who pictures every wave as a sideways (transverse) motion picks this. The student's hand moves along the slinky, so the coils are displaced along the slinky too: the disturbance is parallel to the direction of travel.

A student who thinks a wave carries the medium with it picks this. The wave transfers energy to the far end, but each coil only moves back and forth about its own position and stays in the middle of the slinky.

Pushing and pulling the end along the slinky makes a longitudinal wave: each coil is displaced parallel to the direction the wave travels, moving back and forth about its equilibrium position. The wave shows as regions of bunched-up and spread-out coils.

A student who thinks each part of the medium follows the shape of the wave picks this. The coil moves back and forth along one straight line, the length of the slinky; no part of the slinky follows a wavy path.
questions.explain: Pushing and pulling the end along the slinky makes a longitudinal wave: each coil is displaced parallel to the direction the wave travels, moving back and forth about its equilibrium position. The wave shows as regions of bunched-up and spread-out coils.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes a sound wave traveling through air?
options: Air molecules vibrate up and down, perpendicular to the direction of travel.
Electromagnetic waves from the vibrating source travel through the air to the ear.
Sound particles given off by the source travel through the air to the listener.
Air molecules vibrate back and forth along the direction the sound travels.
optionWhy: A student who takes the wavy line of a sound graph as a picture of the motion picks this. The graph plots pressure against time or position; the molecules themselves move along the direction of travel, so sound is longitudinal, not transverse.
A student who groups sound with light and radio picks this. Sound is a mechanical wave, a disturbance of the air itself; unlike an electromagnetic wave, it cannot travel through a vacuum.
A student who pictures sound as a substance of its own picks this. Nothing called a sound particle is emitted: sound is the vibration of the air molecules, passed from each molecule to its neighbors.

Sound is modeled as a mechanical longitudinal wave. The air molecules are the medium; each one vibrates back and forth parallel to the direction the sound travels, producing the compressions and rarefactions that make up the wave.
questions.explain: Sound is modeled as a mechanical longitudinal wave. The air molecules are the medium; each one vibrates back and forth parallel to the direction the sound travels, producing the compressions and rarefactions that make up the wave.

questions.q: The graph shows the air pressure P as a function of position x along a sound wave at one instant. P₀ is the pressure of the undisturbed air, and the vertical axis is broken between 0 and P₀. Which labeled arrow represents the amplitude of the sound wave?
options: Arrow X
Arrow Y
Arrow Z
Arrow W
optionWhy: A student who measures from a trough to a crest picks this. Arrow X spans the maximum decrease and the maximum increase together, twice the amplitude; the amplitude is measured from P₀.

A student who takes the amplitude as the highest pressure reached picks this. Arrow Y runs from zero pressure to a crest, P₀ plus the amplitude. The undisturbed air already has pressure P₀; the amplitude is only the change from P₀.

A student who measures along the wave from one crest to the next picks this. Arrow Z is horizontal, a distance along x between neighboring crests (compressions), which is the wavelength, not the amplitude.

The amplitude of a longitudinal pressure wave is the maximum increase (or decrease) in pressure from the equilibrium pressure P₀. Arrow W runs from the P₀ line up to a crest, the maximum increase above P₀.
questions.explain: The amplitude of a longitudinal pressure wave is the maximum increase (or decrease) in pressure from the equilibrium pressure P₀. Arrow W runs from the P₀ line up to a crest, the maximum increase above P₀.
questions.working: Amplitude = maximum departure from equilibrium pressure P₀ = arrow W (P₀ to crest). X = crest-to-trough (2 × amplitude); Y = from P = 0 to crest (P₀ + amplitude); Z = crest to crest along x (wavelength).

figure.alt: Graph of P on the vertical axis against x on the horizontal axis. The vertical axis starts at 0 and has a break mark between 0 and a dashed horizontal line labeled P₀. A smooth sine-shaped curve oscillates about the P₀ line with equal crests above and troughs below. Four double-headed arrows are drawn: W runs vertically from the P₀ line up to a crest; X runs vertically from a trough up to the level of the crests; Y runs vertically from the horizontal axis at 0 up to a crest; Z runs horizontally from one crest to the next crest.

questions.q: A floating buoy moves up and down as water waves pass it. Which of the following is the period of the waves?
options: The time the buoy takes to go from its highest point back to its highest point
The time the buoy takes to go from its highest point down to its very lowest point
The time a crest takes to travel from the buoy to the shore close by
The number of times the buoy reaches its highest point each second
optionWhy: The period is the time for one complete oscillation. Starting at its highest point, the buoy must go down to its lowest point and come back up to its highest point before its motion starts to repeat.

A student who counts one swing from top to bottom as a whole oscillation picks this. From highest to lowest is only half an oscillation: the buoy has not yet returned to where it started, so this time is half the period.

A student who thinks the period is the time the wave takes to get somewhere picks this. That travel time depends on how far away the shore is and on the wave speed; the period describes how often the motion at one place repeats.
A student who treats period and frequency as the same quantity picks this. The number of repeats each second is the frequency, f; the period is its reciprocal, T = 1/f, the time taken by one repeat.
questions.explain: The period is the time for one complete oscillation. Starting at its highest point, the buoy must go down to its lowest point and come back up to its highest point before its motion starts to repeat.

questions.q: Two sinusoidal waves travel along two identical strings under the same tension. The waves have the same amplitude. Wave X has a frequency of 20 Hz, and wave Y has a frequency of 60 Hz. Which claim about the energy carried by one meter of each wave, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: They carry equal amounts of energy, because the two waves have the same amplitude.
Y carries more energy, because each part of its string moves faster as it oscillates.
X carries more energy, because its wavelength is longer, which makes it a bigger wave.
Y carries more energy, because it travels along its string at the greater speed.
optionWhy: A student who thinks a wave's energy depends only on its amplitude picks this. Energy increases with amplitude, but it also increases with frequency: at equal amplitudes, the parts of string Y oscillate faster and so have more energy.

The energy of a wave increases with its frequency. The amplitudes are equal, so a point on either string moves through the same distance in each cycle, but a point on Y completes three times as many cycles each second. It therefore moves three times as fast on average and has more kinetic energy, so each meter of wave Y carries more energy.

A student who links a longer wavelength with a bigger, more energetic wave picks this. X's wavelength is three times as long because its frequency is one third as great; at the same amplitude, the lower-frequency wave carries less energy, not more.

A student who thinks higher-frequency waves travel faster picks this. The strings are identical and under the same tension, so the two waves travel at the same speed and Y simply has the shorter wavelength. Y does carry more energy, but because its string oscillates faster, not because the wave moves faster.
questions.explain: The energy of a wave increases with its frequency. The amplitudes are equal, so a point on either string moves through the same distance in each cycle, but a point on Y completes three times as many cycles each second. It therefore moves three times as fast on average and has more kinetic energy, so each meter of wave Y carries more energy.

questions.q: A wave travels along a string at 1.5 m/s. The graph shows the displacement y of one point on the string as a function of time t. What is the wavelength of the wave?
optionWhy: A student who reads the graph as a picture of the string picks this, taking the horizontal length of one cycle as the wavelength. The horizontal axis is time, so 0.40 s is the period. The wavelength is the distance the wave travels in one period: (1.5 m/s)(0.40 s) = 0.60 m.

A student who takes the period as the time between successive zero crossings, 0.20 s, picks this: (1.5 m/s)(0.20 s) = 0.30 m. Between those crossings the point makes only half an oscillation; a full oscillation takes 0.40 s.

The motion repeats every 0.40 s (for example, y = 0 moving upward at t = 0 and again at t = 0.40 s), so T = 0.40 s and f = 1/T = 2.5 Hz. The wavelength is λ = v/f = (1.5 m/s)/(2.5 Hz) = 0.60 m: in one period the wave travels 0.60 m.
A student who counts the three cycles on the graph and calls the frequency 3 Hz picks this: (1.5 m/s)/(3 Hz) = 0.50 m. The three cycles take 1.20 s, so the frequency is 3/(1.20 s) = 2.5 Hz.
questions.explain: The motion repeats every 0.40 s (for example, y = 0 moving upward at t = 0 and again at t = 0.40 s), so T = 0.40 s and f = 1/T = 2.5 Hz. The wavelength is λ = v/f = (1.5 m/s)/(2.5 Hz) = 0.60 m: in one period the wave travels 0.60 m.
questions.working: The graph repeats every 0.40 s (zero crossings moving upward at t = 0, 0.40 s, 0.80 s, 1.20 s), so T = 0.40 s and f = 1/T = 2.5 Hz. λ = v/f = vT = (1.5 m/s)(0.40 s) = 0.60 m.

figure.alt: Graph of displacement y (cm) against time t (s) for one point on the string. The vertical axis is marked 2.0, 0 and −2.0; the horizontal axis is marked 0.20, 0.40, 0.60, 0.80, 1.00 and 1.20, with a vertical gridline at each mark. The curve is a sine wave that starts at y = 0 at t = 0, rises to 2.0 at t = 0.10 s, returns to 0 at t = 0.20 s, falls to −2.0 at t = 0.30 s and is back at 0 at t = 0.40 s. It repeats this pattern exactly, so three complete cycles are shown between t = 0 and t = 1.20 s.

questions.q: The graph shows the shape of a string at one instant as a wave of frequency 4.0 Hz travels along it. What is the speed of the wave?
optionWhy: A student who takes the wavelength as the distance from a crest to the next trough, 0.40 m, picks this: (4.0 Hz)(0.40 m) = 1.6 m/s. Crest to trough is half a wavelength; crest to next crest is 0.80 m.

A student who takes the wavelength as the length of the whole wave shown, 1.60 m, picks this: (4.0 Hz)(1.60 m) = 6.4 m/s. The graph shows two repeats of the pattern; one repeat, 0.80 m, is the wavelength.
A student who uses λ = f/v, and so v = f/λ, picks this: (4.0 Hz)/(0.80 m) = 5.0. The correct relation is λ = v/f, so v = fλ = 3.2 m/s; f/λ does not even have the units of a speed.
Successive crests are at x = 0.20 m and x = 1.00 m, so the wavelength is 0.80 m. v = fλ = (4.0 Hz)(0.80 m) = 3.2 m/s.
questions.explain: Successive crests are at x = 0.20 m and x = 1.00 m, so the wavelength is 0.80 m. v = fλ = (4.0 Hz)(0.80 m) = 3.2 m/s.
questions.working: From the graph, successive crests are at x = 0.20 m and x = 1.00 m, so λ = 0.80 m. v = fλ = (4.0 Hz)(0.80 m) = 3.2 m/s.

figure.alt: Snapshot graph of the displacement y (cm) of the string against position x (m) along it at one instant. The vertical axis is marked 5.0, 0 and −5.0; the horizontal axis is marked 0.40, 0.80, 1.20 and 1.60, with a vertical gridline every 0.20 m. The string lies between x = 0 and x = 1.60 m. Its shape is a sine curve that starts at y = 0 at x = 0, has crests (y = 5.0 cm) at x = 0.20 m and 1.00 m, troughs (y = −5.0 cm) at x = 0.60 m and 1.40 m, and crosses y = 0 at x = 0.40, 0.80 and 1.20 m, ending at y = 0 at x = 1.60 m.

questions.q: Sound from a loudspeaker in air reaches the surface of a swimming pool, and sound travels on into the water. Which property of the sound is the same in the water as in the air?
options: The distance between its adjacent compressions
The distance it travels in each second
The amount of energy it carries each second
The number of oscillations it makes each second
optionWhy: A student who thinks the wavelength is kept when a wave enters a new medium picks this. The distance between compressions is the wavelength, λ = v/f; the frequency is unchanged, but sound travels about four times as fast in water as in air, so the wavelength in water is about four times as long.
A student who thinks a wave keeps the speed its source gave it picks this. The speed of sound is set by the medium: sound travels about four times as fast in water as in air.

A student who thinks all of the sound passes into the water picks this. Part of the sound is reflected at the surface (for air and water, most of it), so the energy carried into the water each second is less than the energy arriving at the surface each second.

The frequency of a wave does not change when it travels from one medium to another. Each compression that reaches the surface produces one compression in the water, so the water oscillates as many times each second as the air does.
questions.explain: The frequency of a wave does not change when it travels from one medium to another. Each compression that reaches the surface produces one compression in the water, so the water oscillates as many times each second as the air does.

questions.q: A transverse wave on a long rope is described as polarized. What does this mean?
options: The wave travels in a single direction, away from its source.
Each point of the rope oscillates back and forth along the rope's length.
The rope oscillates in a single plane, for example up and down only.
The wave has a single frequency, so its crests are equally spaced.
optionWhy: A student who thinks polarization describes the direction of travel picks this. Every wave on a rope travels along the rope; polarization describes the direction of the oscillations, which for a polarized wave is one direction perpendicular to the rope.

A student who thinks a polarized wave oscillates along its direction of travel picks this. Oscillation along the rope would make a longitudinal wave, which cannot be polarized; a polarized transverse wave oscillates in one direction perpendicular to the rope.

A polarized transverse wave oscillates in a single plane: every point of the rope moves back and forth along the same direction (for example, only up and down), perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels.

A student who confuses polarization with having a single frequency picks this. A wave of one frequency can oscillate in many directions, and a wave oscillating in one plane can contain several frequencies; polarization refers only to the direction of oscillation.
questions.explain: A polarized transverse wave oscillates in a single plane: every point of the rope moves back and forth along the same direction (for example, only up and down), perpendicular to the direction in which the wave travels.

questions.q: A pulse carrying energy E₀ travels along a light string toward the knot that joins it to a heavy string. The two strings are under the same tension. Which claim about the energy E_T of the pulse on the heavy string after the pulse reaches the knot, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: E_T is less than E₀, since part of the energy goes into a reflected pulse.
E_T is less than E₀, since the pulse slows down on the heavy string.
E_T is equal to E₀, since the whole pulse passes into the heavy string.
E_T is zero, since the heavy string reflects the entire pulse straight back.
optionWhy: At the knot the pulse is partly reflected and partly transmitted. Energy is conserved, so E₀ is shared: the reflected pulse carries some of it back along the light string, and the transmitted pulse carries the rest, so E_T < E₀.

A student who treats the pulse like an object whose energy falls when it slows down picks this. The transmitted pulse does travel more slowly, but that is not why E_T is less than E₀: the missing energy is carried back along the light string by the reflected pulse. A pulse passing from a heavy string into a light one speeds up, yet it too transmits less than all of its energy, for the same reason.
A student who thinks joined strings pass the whole wave on picks this. Wherever the wave speed changes, part of the wave is reflected, so the heavy string receives only part of the energy.

A student who pictures the heavy string as a wall picks this. The heavy string can move, so a pulse is transmitted along it as well as reflected; only an end that cannot move reflects the whole pulse.
questions.explain: At the knot the pulse is partly reflected and partly transmitted. Energy is conserved, so E₀ is shared: the reflected pulse carries some of it back along the light string, and the transmitted pulse carries the rest, so E_T < E₀.

questions.q: In each diagram, the arrow shows the direction in which a wave travels and the other lines are drawn to represent the wave. In which diagram are the lines the wave fronts of a plane wave?
options: Diagram Q
Diagram P
Diagram R
Diagram S
optionWhy: A student who draws wave fronts along the direction of travel, like rays, picks this. Lines parallel to the direction of travel are rays; wave fronts are perpendicular to it.

The wave fronts of a plane wave are flat, parallel to one another and perpendicular to the direction of travel. In a diagram they appear as straight, parallel lines drawn across the direction of travel, as in P.

A student who thinks a plane wave spreads out across a flat surface, like ripples on a pond, picks this. Circular wave fronts spread out from a point; a plane wave's wave fronts are straight and parallel.

A student who thinks a plane wave is an oscillation drawn in one flat plane picks this. A single sine curve is a graph of the field along the line of travel; 'plane' refers to the flat shape of the wave fronts.
questions.explain: The wave fronts of a plane wave are flat, parallel to one another and perpendicular to the direction of travel. In a diagram they appear as straight, parallel lines drawn across the direction of travel, as in P.

figure.alt: Four panels labeled P, Q, R and S, each containing an arrow at the bottom pointing to the right. Panel P: five straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines, each perpendicular to the arrow. Panel Q: four straight, parallel lines, each parallel to the arrow. Panel R: three concentric circles around a dot. Panel S: a single sine-shaped curve running from left to right, along the direction of the arrow.

questions.q: X-rays and radio waves are both electromagnetic waves. Which property distinguishes the two categories?
options: Their speed in a vacuum, which is much greater for X-rays
Their amplitude, which is much greater for X-rays
Their nature: X-rays are particles, and radio waves are waves
Their wavelength, which is much shorter for X-rays
optionWhy: A student who thinks higher-frequency electromagnetic waves travel faster picks this. Every electromagnetic wave travels at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum; X-rays differ from radio waves in wavelength and frequency.
A student who links X-rays' high energy with a large amplitude picks this. The category is set by wavelength; a weak X-ray beam is still X-rays and a strong radio signal is still radio waves.
A student who thinks X-rays are particles rather than light-like waves picks this. X-rays are electromagnetic waves, as radio waves are; they sit at the short-wavelength end of the same spectrum.
The categories of electromagnetic waves are characterized by their wavelengths. X-rays have far shorter wavelengths (and so far higher frequencies) than radio waves; in a vacuum both travel at c.
questions.explain: The categories of electromagnetic waves are characterized by their wavelengths. X-rays have far shorter wavelengths (and so far higher frequencies) than radio waves; in a vacuum both travel at c.

questions.q: A physics textbook uses the term 'electromagnetic radiation'. Which waves does this term include?
options: The particles and rays that radioactive materials give off
Waves of every wavelength, from radio waves to gamma rays
The invisible waves, such as ultraviolet, but not visible light
Infrared waves, which are the kind of radiation that carries heat
optionWhy: A student who reads 'radiation' as nuclear radiation picks this. In 'electromagnetic radiation' the word means energy carried by electromagnetic waves of any wavelength; alpha and beta particles are not electromagnetic waves at all.

Electromagnetic waves of all wavelengths, visible light included, are collectively called electromagnetic radiation (and sometimes light). Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays all qualify.
A student who thinks 'radiation' means only invisible waves picks this. Visible light is electromagnetic radiation too; it lies between infrared and ultraviolet on the same spectrum.
A student who equates radiation with heat radiation picks this. Infrared is one category of electromagnetic radiation; the term covers every category, from radio waves to gamma rays.
questions.explain: Electromagnetic waves of all wavelengths, visible light included, are collectively called electromagnetic radiation (and sometimes light). Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays all qualify.

questions.q: Two loudspeakers side by side emit sound continuously, one at 300 Hz and the other at 500 Hz. Which statement about the two sound waves, in the region where both are present, is correct?
options: They do not interfere, because waves of different frequencies pass through without interacting.
They interfere just at the points where a crest of one wave meets a crest of the other.
They interfere: at each point the air's displacement is the sum of both displacements.
They do not interfere, because the louder wave takes over wherever the two overlap.
optionWhy: A student who thinks interference requires equal frequencies picks this. Steady interference patterns do need matched frequencies, but any overlapping waves interact: their displacements add. Beats are interference between waves of different frequencies.
A student who thinks interference happens only at special points picks this. Superposition applies at every point where the waves overlap; crest-on-crest points are just where the result is largest.

Interference is the interaction of any waves that overlap; they need not share a frequency. Wherever both waves are present, the displacement of the air is the sum of the displacements each would produce alone. Because the frequencies differ, the waves move in and out of step and the combined disturbance keeps changing, but they still interfere.
A student who thinks the stronger wave overrides the weaker one picks this. Neither wave takes over: both displacements are present and add, so the quieter wave still changes the result.
questions.explain: Interference is the interaction of any waves that overlap; they need not share a frequency. Wherever both waves are present, the displacement of the air is the sum of the displacements each would produce alone. Because the frequencies differ, the waves move in and out of step and the combined disturbance keeps changing, but they still interfere.

questions.q: The diagram shows a long rope at one instant, with pulse P moving right and pulse Q moving left, as the arrows show. The horizontal grid lines are equally spaced. Which statement describes the rope after the pulses have completely passed each other?
options: P, still upright, is to the left of Q and moves left; Q, still inverted, moves right.
A single upright pulse, half as tall as P, is left on the rope and keeps moving along it.
P moves right with its shape unchanged, and Q has been absorbed into P.
P, still upright, is to the right of Q and moves right; Q, still inverted, moves left.
optionWhy: A student who pictures the pulses as objects that collide and bounce back picks this. Pulses are disturbances of the rope, not objects: they overlap and pass through each other, so P keeps moving right and ends up to the right of Q.

A student who thinks the combined shape formed during the overlap stays on the rope picks this. The sum of two grid spaces up and one grid space down exists only while the pulses overlap; once they separate, each pulse reappears with its original shape.
A student who thinks the larger pulse overwhelms the smaller one picks this. Neither pulse absorbs the other: Q emerges unchanged, still inverted and one grid space deep, moving left.

Pulses pass through each other. While they overlap the displacements add, but afterward each pulse continues in its original direction with its original shape: P, upright and two grid spaces tall, is now on the right moving right, and Q, inverted and one grid space deep, is on the left moving left.
questions.explain: Pulses pass through each other. While they overlap the displacements add, but afterward each pulse continues in its original direction with its original shape: P, upright and two grid spaces tall, is now on the right moving right, and Q, inverted and one grid space deep, is on the left moving left.
questions.working: Pulses pass through each other unchanged. After passing: P (upright, height 2 grid spaces) is on the right moving right; Q (inverted, depth 1 grid space) is on the left moving left.

On the right, pulse Q is a downward dip one grid space below the rope's level; an arrow below it points left. The pulses have not yet reached each other.

questions.q: Two tuning forks, of frequencies 440 Hz and 444 Hz, are struck together. A listener hears the loudness rise and fall four times each second. Which statement correctly explains this?
options: The sound given out by each fork on its own grows louder and quieter four times each second.
The two waves combine into a new sound wave of frequency 4 Hz, which is heard as the pulsing.
Waves of different frequencies cannot interfere, so the ear switches back and forth between the two sounds.
The waves drift in and out of step, so their displacements alternately add together and oppose.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the pulsing is in the sources picks this. Each fork alone gives a steady tone that fades only slowly; the rise and fall appears only when both sound together, because it comes from their interference.

A student who thinks the beat is a separate low-frequency wave picks this. The combined wave still oscillates at about 442 Hz; what changes four times a second is its amplitude, heard as the loudness rising and falling.

A student who thinks only waves of equal frequency interfere picks this. Waves of any frequencies superpose where they overlap; beats are the result of that superposition for two slightly different frequencies.

Because the frequencies differ slightly, the waves are in phase at some instants (displacements in the same direction: constructive interference, loud) and out of phase a little later (opposite displacements: destructive interference, quiet). The cycle repeats |444 Hz − 440 Hz| = 4 times each second.
questions.explain: Because the frequencies differ slightly, the waves are in phase at some instants (displacements in the same direction: constructive interference, loud) and out of phase a little later (opposite displacements: destructive interference, quiet). The cycle repeats |444 Hz − 440 Hz| = 4 times each second.

questions.q: A narrow beam of light in air strikes the flat top surface of a thick block of clear glass at an angle of incidence of 30°. Which statement describes what happens to the light?
options: Some is reflected and some enters the glass, where a small part of it is absorbed.
None of it is reflected; all of it enters the glass, which is clear rather than shiny.
All of it is reflected or all is transmitted, with the angle deciding which one.
Some is reflected and the rest crosses the block, since clear glass absorbs no light.
optionWhy: At a boundary between media with different indices of refraction, the light divides: part is reflected and part is transmitted into the glass. Glass is not perfectly transparent, so a small part of the transmitted light is absorbed as it travels through the thick block; the reflected, transmitted and absorbed parts together account for all of the incident light.

A student who thinks only shiny surfaces reflect light picks this. Clear glass reflects part of the light at its surface (about 4% at normal incidence), which is why you can see faint reflections in a window.

A student who pictures light at a boundary as going one way or the other picks this. The light divides at the surface at any angle of incidence; all-or-nothing reflection happens only in total internal reflection, which needs light traveling toward a smaller index, not from air into glass.

A student who thinks only dark materials absorb light picks this. Clear glass absorbs a small fraction of the light passing through it, more for a thicker block; a thick slab of window glass looks green when viewed through its edge.
questions.explain: At a boundary between media with different indices of refraction, the light divides: part is reflected and part is transmitted into the glass. Glass is not perfectly transparent, so a small part of the transmitted light is absorbed as it travels through the thick block; the reflected, transmitted and absorbed parts together account for all of the incident light.

questions.q: A student wants to predict whether light traveling in one transparent medium undergoes a 180° phase change when it reflects from a second transparent medium. Which information does the student need?
options: The index of refraction of the second medium, from which the light reflects
Which of the two media has the greater mass density, the first or the second
How the index of refraction of the second medium compares with that of the first
The thickness of the second medium and the wavelength of the light used
optionWhy: A student who treats the phase change as a property of the reflecting material picks this. The same material can give either result: light in air reflecting from glass changes phase, but light in diamond reflecting from glass does not. The index of the first medium is needed for the comparison.
A student who reads 'denser medium' as a medium of greater mass density picks this. The comparison is between indices of refraction: oil is less dense than water but can have the greater index.

The phase change on reflection depends on the relative indices of the two media: light reflected from a medium of greater index changes phase by 180°, and light reflected from a medium of smaller index does not. Both indices are needed to make the comparison.

A student who mixes up the phase change on reflection with the phase difference from the extra path in a film picks this. Thickness and wavelength matter for the path difference; the phase change on reflection depends only on the two indices.
questions.explain: The phase change on reflection depends on the relative indices of the two media: light reflected from a medium of greater index changes phase by 180°, and light reflected from a medium of smaller index does not. Both indices are needed to make the comparison.

questions.q: Light traveling in air passes into a block of glass at normal incidence. Which statement about the light transmitted into the glass is correct?
options: Its phase shifts by 180° at the boundary, as glass has the greater index.
Its frequency decreases in the glass, because it travels more slowly there.
Its phase is continuous across the boundary, with no 180° shift.
Its wavelength is unchanged in the glass, because its color does not change.
optionWhy: A student who applies the reflection rule to transmitted light picks this. The 180° change happens to the light reflected from the glass; the light transmitted into the glass has no phase change.
A student who links a smaller speed to a smaller frequency picks this. The frequency is set by the source and is the same in air and in glass; the smaller speed goes with a shorter wavelength, λ/n.

Refraction does not change the phase of a wave: the transmitted wave continues from the incident wave without a sudden shift. Its speed and wavelength change in the glass, but its frequency does not. A 180° phase change can happen only to the reflected light.

A student who ties each color to one fixed wavelength picks this. In the glass the light is slower at the same frequency, so its wavelength is shorter, λ/n; it has the same color again when it leaves.
questions.explain: Refraction does not change the phase of a wave: the transmitted wave continues from the incident wave without a sudden shift. Its speed and wavelength change in the glass, but its frequency does not. A 180° phase change can happen only to the reflected light.
questions.working: Refraction leaves the phase continuous (no 180° shift); f is unchanged, v = c/n and λ_n = λ/n decrease.
